intro: Roosendaal's registered trees stand in four public places across town. De Kring square holds a pair of planes: a rare Oriental plane from around 1850, the wilder parent of the London plane, with a London plane from the 1900s about 13 metres in front of it. Emile van Loonpark holds a horse chestnut behind the pond that flowers every May. On Burgerhoutsestraat a catalpa and a London plane frame the same building from opposite sides, and in the old cemetery on Bachlaan a double-flowered horse chestnut from the 1870s stands alone among the graves.
meta_description: Six registered trees in Roosendaal: an Oriental and a London plane paired at De Kring, a chestnut among the Bachlaan graves, and a catalpa.
question_meta: Roosendaal's oldest tree is an Oriental plane at De Kring, banded to around 1850 and roughly 180 years old. Its story and five more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Roosendaal is the Oriental Plane of De Kring, which the national tree register bands to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. It stands on De Kring square, a rare tree in a country whose squares are planted with London planes.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every figure on this page is a band. The register is the single source throughout, so every entry ships flagged rather than confirmed. The six trees sit in four spots. De Kring square holds the Oriental plane, a species planted far less often in the Netherlands than its hybrid offspring, the London plane, with a London plane from the 1900s 13 metres in front; the horse chestnut that shared the square with them was felled in 2014 and a young tree planted in its place. Emile van Loonpark holds a horse chestnut behind the pond, from around 1870. Burgerhoutsestraat holds a catalpa and a London plane at opposite corners of the same building, the catalpa flowering white in midsummer and hanging its long bean pods into winter. The Algemene Begraafplaats on Bachlaan holds a double-flowered horse chestnut banded to the 1870s. All six stand on public ground with nothing to pay; the cemetery is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30. Where a pin is marked approximate, we know the site and not the exact trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Roosendaal?
faq.a: The Oriental Plane of De Kring, banded by the national tree register to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. It stands on De Kring square, in the middle of town.

faq.q: What happened to the old lime in Emile van Loonpark?
faq.a: The national register records it as declared dead in 1998. The park's horse chestnut, behind the pond, is still there.

faq.q: Why does an Oriental plane at De Kring stand out?
faq.a: Most planes planted on Dutch squares are London planes, a hybrid bred from the Oriental species and an American one. This is the wilder-growing parent itself, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, planted here around 1850.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Every tree on this list stands on a public square, park, street or cemetery with nothing to pay. The cemetery on Bachlaan is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30; the others can be seen at any time.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of De Kring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 180 years, from a registered planting date around 1850
trees.story:
This Oriental plane stands by De Kring, a public square in Roosendaal, banded by the national register to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. A horse chestnut of about the same age once shared the square with it; the register records that tree felled in 2014 and a young one planted in its place, which leaves the plane as the oldest trunk on De Kring. A London plane from around 1900 to 1910 stands about 13 metres east, in front of it.

Oriental plane is the older, wilder-growing parent of the hybrid London plane that lines so many European streets, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, and it is planted less often in the Netherlands than its more tolerant offspring. Left to grow on an open square rather than pruned to a street profile, an Oriental plane develops the same flaking, camouflage-patterned bark as its hybrid relative but with a more irregular, spreading crown, often leaning and forking low rather than rising in a single clean trunk.

The register records the species and the decade but nothing of who planted it or why, which is typical for a tree whose interest is simply having survived on the same square for nearly two centuries while whatever stood around it changed. If you know more of De Kring's own history, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the back one of the two old planes in this corner of De Kring, 4.5 metres round. The younger London plane stands about 13 metres east, in front of it.

trees.name: The Catalpa of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.story:
This catalpa stands southwest of a building on Burgerhoutsestraat, banded by the national register to a planting around 1900, roughly 130 years old. A London plane the register also lists grows at the front of the same building, so the property carries two registered trees framing it from different sides, one native to the eastern United States and one a hybrid bred in seventeenth century Europe.

Southern catalpa is grown for its broad, heart-shaped leaves and, through midsummer, loose clusters of white flowers marked with purple and yellow spots inside each throat, followed by long, bean-like seed pods that can hang on the bare branches well into winter, giving the species its other common name, Indian bean tree, despite having no connection to India.

A catalpa at 130 years is well into a mature specimen's proportions, wide-crowned and often leaning or multi-stemmed if it was ever cut back hard when young. The register records nothing of who planted it or why, only the species and the decade. If you know more about this tree or the building it stands beside, tell us.

best_time.label: July, when the orchid-like flowers open in loose clusters across the crown

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad heart-shaped leaves and the long bean-like pods that hang on into winter. It stands southwest of the building at Burgerhoutsestraat 12; the registered tree at the front is a plane.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Pond
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Roosendaal, Emile van Loonpark, achter vijver

trees.story:
This horse chestnut stands behind the pond in Emile van Loonpark, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. The park once held an older tree still, a Dutch lime the register bands to somewhere between 1750 and 1800, but the register records that lime as declared dead in 1998, so this chestnut is the park's registered veteran now.

A horse chestnut planted beside water has usually had reliable growing conditions its whole life, and at 160 years this one should show the full domed crown and heavy branch structure the species develops when left largely alone. Every May it produces the upright white flower spikes chestnuts are planted for across Europe, and reflected in the pond behind it, the display reads differently than a chestnut standing on hard pavement elsewhere in this list.

The register gives no further history for this tree, only species and decade. Emile van Loonpark is public and open daily, and this chestnut is the reason to walk to the far side of the pond rather than stopping at the park's edge. If you know more about it, tell us.

best_time.label: May, when the white flower spikes cover the crown and reflect in the pond

trees.verify_notes: 2026-09-08: the story claimed the park's lime was declared dead in 1998 and that this chestnut was therefore the park's surviving veteran. Both halves are wrong. The Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen still carries nr 1680922, Hollandse linde, Emile van Loonpark, band 1750-1800, and it is not among the register's dead entries. We publish that lime ourselves as roo_010, so the page contradicted its own neighbour. Sentence replaced with what the register says. 2026-10-12: reversed. The live LRMB layer now carries nr 1680922 as status 5, Dood/geveld, with 'In 1998 al dood verklaard' and an inspector's 'onvindbaar' on 2018-08-29; roo_010 was retired the same day and the story says the lime is gone.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the white flower candles in May, reflected in the water behind it. It stands on the far side of the pond in Emile van Loonpark, so keep walking rather than stopping at the park's edge.

trees.name: The Plane of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Roosendaal, Burgerhoutsestraat 12, aan de voorzijde van het gebouw

trees.story:
This London plane stands at the front of the same Burgerhoutsestraat building whose southwest corner holds a registered catalpa, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old and a generation younger than its catalpa neighbour on the other side of the same property.

London plane is the hybrid that resulted from crossing an American and an Oriental species in seventeenth century Europe, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, air pollution and hard pruning better than almost any other large tree available, which is why it became the default choice for European streets and squares from the eighteenth century onward. Its bark flakes away in patches rather than splitting, leaving a mottled grey, green and cream pattern across the trunk that keeps changing as old plates drop and new bark shows through underneath.

At the front of a building rather than tucked behind it, this plane has likely had more pruning against passing traffic than its catalpa neighbour, which a plane tolerates without much complaint. The register records only species and decade. If you know the building's own history, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark, flaking away in patches to leave a mottled grey, green and cream trunk. It stands at the front of the building at Burgerhoutsestraat 12; the catalpa is round at the southwest corner.

trees.name: The London Plane of De Kring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 120 years, from a registered planting decade
trees.access: Free. Public square (plein) owned by the municipality, register: visitable ja, visible ja, openbaar ja. No hours; open at all times.
trees.transport: Roosendaal station is about 0.8 km north, roughly a 10 minute walk via Stationsstraat and Kerkstraat.
trees.story:
The national tree register describes this London plane by the tree behind it. About 13 metres west stands the Oriental plane of De Kring, one of the two species the London plane was bred from, so this corner of the square puts a hybrid and its parent side by side.

This is the front tree and the younger of the pair, banded by the register to a planting between 1900 and 1910, which makes it roughly 116 to 126 years old. The register gives it 25 metres of height to the Oriental plane's 22, and a trunk 3.6 metres round at chest height.

The pair have not had an easy century. In 2002 the Bomenstichting, the Dutch tree foundation, studied the ground beneath them and advised keeping both planes. Building went ahead anyway, inside the spread of their crowns and their roots. When the register last checked, in July 2023, it was mostly the Oriental plane behind whose crown had gone thin, with dead tips on its branches. This one is not the tree it describes as declining.

A horse chestnut once made this a trio. The register records it felled in 2014 and a young tree planted in its place, so that young tree is not part of the old group.

The register is the only source for this tree, and July 2023 is the last time it was recorded standing. If you have walked past it since, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the front one of the two old planes in this corner of De Kring, in its own round tree pit. The rarer Oriental plane stands about 13 metres west, behind it.

trees.name: The Baumann's Horse Chestnut of the Algemene Begraafplaats
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150 years, from a registered planting decade

location.address: Roosendaal, Bachlaan 1, Algemene Begraafplaats (closed municipal cemetery)

verified_sources: https://lokaleregelgeving.overheid.nl/CVDR10613 (Verordening op het beheer en het gebruik van de gesloten gemeentelijke begraafplaatsen, art. 2 para 1: open to everyone daily 8.00 to 16.30)
trees.access: Free. Municipal closed cemetery, open to everyone daily 8.00 to 16.30 (municipal cemetery regulation, art. 2; Oorlogsgraf.nl gives the same hours and says dogs are not allowed). Register: visitable ja, owner gemeente.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km east of Roosendaal station, roughly a 20 minute walk via Bredaseweg; parking for about 10 cars in front of the cemetery.
trees.story:
Every May this horse chestnut covers itself in white flowers, and every autumn it drops not a single conker. It is 'Baumannii', the double-flowered clone of the ordinary horse chestnut, and its flowers set no fruit.

The national tree register bands its planting to the 1870s, roughly 146 to 156 years ago. Sources disagree on when the Algemene Begraafplaats itself opened, somewhere between about 1880 and 1894, so the tree may be as old as the cemetery or older. Nobody has recorded how it came to stand here.

It has seen the cemetery's whole working life. Roosendaal buried its dead here until 1978, when the ground closed to new burials, and the chestnut stayed on among the grave rows, alone, 18 metres tall and 3.64 metres round at chest height.

Age has left its mark. The register notes a split in the main fork with small cracks beneath it, and in December 1999 the crown was thinned and anchored. It was inspected again in May 2025 and is still listed as monumental.

That register is the only record of this tree we have found; if you know its history, tell us. The cemetery is open daily from 8.00 to 16.30, and dogs are not allowed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone big horse chestnut among the grave rows, 3.64 metres round, with no other crown within about 8 metres. In May its flowers are double, and in autumn it bears no conkers.

best_time.label: May, when double white flower candles cover the crown
